newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia on brink, if tax revenues refuse to rise.
newsitem.headline: Russia on brink, if tax revenues refuse to rise.

text.p: Low and illusory tax revenues threaten the Russian government with catastrophe but it is determined to improve the situation substantially, government officials said on Wednesday.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said Russia met only 49 percent of the tax receipts target set for the first quarter, although government debts cancelled in lieu of cash tax payments raised the total receipts to 69 percent of the target.
Kulikov said real monetary receipts were about flat compared to the first quarter of last year and that debt cancellation was now 44 percent of total tax receipts.
"If debt cancellation (as payment) exceeds 50 percent, the government is on the edge of bankruptcy," Kulikov told a news conference.
State Tax Service chief Alexander Pochinok said he hoped to bring collection rates to 90 percent by the summer but that failure to raise revenues would be a disaster for Russia.
"Either the government is able to support itself, or catastrophe awaits," he told a news conference.

An International Monetary Fund (IMF) monitoring team is in Moscow to consider renewing tranche payments of its $10 billion three-year loan, which has been in effect suspended for a several months because of low tax collection.

President Boris Yeltsin appointed a young team of reformers to the government last month, encouraging international investors and IMF managing director Michel Camdessus who said soon afterwards it was time to resume lending.
But he also said the Russian government would need to pass a new tax code to parliament, which Yeltsin has ordered done by the end of this month, before tranche payments resume.

Pochinok says a new, simplified tax code would sharply improve tax collection. But many government and parliamentary officials doubt the code will be passed by 1998 and critics say the present draft does not radically improve efficiency.

Kulikov, who has been given a brief to ebnforce tax collection and crack down on evasion, and Pochinok vowed to work together more closely. They said illegal alcohol imports were costing the treasury dozens of trillions of roubles.

The 1997 budget foresees 434 trillion roubles of revenues and 529.8 trillion roubles expenditures. Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais said budget shortfalls this year could be 100 trillion roubles and is due shortly to suggest massive spending cuts to the government and parliament.

Pochinok said Russia must take on its largest tax debtors, a vow senior government officials have made for more than a year, and that major companies could be forced to issue and transfer new shares to the government as part of arrears restructuring.
Norilsk Nickel metals group's main plant has already said it intends to issue new shares.
"If the owner cannot effectively manage the property, if the owner owes us...then in exceptional cases we should facilitate a change of ownership," Pochinok said.
